reading.body:
Amazon Web Services recorded $717 billion in revenue in 2025 while operating two major AI product lines: SageMaker for full-stack ML lifecycle management and Bedrock for managed foundation model access.

AWS sits at the intersection of compute supply and AI demand. SageMaker's architecture—unified data lakes, model monitoring, bias detection, and governance tools—reflects the infrastructure required to run production AI at scale. Bedrock's API model with VPC support and IAM integration suggests AWS is positioning itself as the managed layer between foundation models and enterprise users who want isolation and control. Both products point to a company treating AI not as a feature but as a platform business spanning data, compute, and model serving.

The scale here matters for power and buildings. A $717 billion revenue company in cloud services operates data centers globally to deliver these products. The fact that SageMaker includes toxicity detection, guardrails, and data lineage tracking indicates AWS is building compliance and observability into the compute layer itself. This is not decorative. As regulatory exposure grows, the infrastructure provider that bakes governance into the platform gains advantage over those that bolt it on later.

The data does not specify AWS's capital spending, energy consumption, or data center locations. It does not break out AI revenue from total AWS revenue or show whether SageMaker and Bedrock are growing faster than legacy services. It does not name which foundation models Bedrock serves or how much compute AWS allocates to these two products versus others.

profile_text.body:
Amazon Web Services describes the next generation of Amazon SageMaker as the center for all data, analytics, and AI. Per the company's site, SageMaker Unified Studio brings AWS machine learning and analytics capabilities into a single development environment with access to data held in data lakes, data warehouses, and third-party or federated sources. The site lists SageMaker AI, including HyperPod, JumpStart, and MLOps, for model development, alongside Amazon Q Developer, which the company describes as its generative AI assistant for software development. It also describes a lakehouse architecture spanning Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift, Apache Iceberg-compatible tools and engines, zero-ETL integrations, governance through Amazon SageMaker Catalog, and open source frameworks on Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue. The site quotes Carrier and an unnamed automotive customer about using SageMaker to unify and govern data and to build lakehouse implementations.

The company's products include Amazon SageMaker, described as full ML lifecycle management with model monitoring, bias detection, and explainability tools, and AWS Bedrock, a managed foundation model API service with IAM integration, VPC support, model evaluation tools, and AgentCore for agent orchestration.

The profile lists Amazon Web Services as a public company founded in 1994, headquartered in Seattle, WA, USA, with ticker AMZN and CIK 0001018724. Its most recent revenue filing is a 10-K for the period ending 2025-12-31, reporting 716924000000 US dollars. Its law exposure is recorded in Washington with a count of 102, and a case associated with the company is Haugland v. Anthropic PBC, in the District Court, D. Delaware.
